utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody again this morning. May the Registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case numb IT-04-83-T number, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And may we have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis and Laurie Sartorio. We are assisted today by our intern, Shona McJarrett, and our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and with me is Nicholas Robson representing General Rasim Delic, together with our case assistants, Lana Deljkic and Lejla Gluhic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before we begin, let me just remind you, sir, at the beginning of your testimony you made a declaration to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. Just to remind you that you are still bound by that declaration to tell the truth. Thank you very much. Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just a minute, before you start?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess I need to announce that, once again, we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis because Judge Harhoff is involved in an initial appearance of an accused in another court. Thank you very much. You may proceed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like the usher to show the witness Exhibit -- pre-trial Exhibit P02152 [Realtime transcript read in error "P02552"].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May we show the witness that exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell us what this document is, if you know?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a list.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: A list of what?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says here, the list of the 3rd Corps, El Mujahedin Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And the date of the document is?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 12th of -- I can't see the next digit. 1995. It may be January or December 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, could you please look at the pages of the document and tell us if you see your name; and if you do, what number it is beside your name?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's listed under 10 -- no, no, 11. Alic, Mustafa Hasib. It's number 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And is all the information on that line correct?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 15th of May, 1993. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this document as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence has a concern over this particular document. As it's just been mentioned, the date of the document is unclear. We'd also point out there doesn't appear to be any cover sheet on it; there doesn't seem to be anything relating to the document to explain who it was sent by or who it was sent to, if anyone; and there doesn't appear to be any sort of official stamp. So we express those concerns, Your Honour, and we would suggest that perhaps the document is not entered into evidence at this stage, unless perhaps we can explore those concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm advised, in fact, that it is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Right. Your Honour, the reason I said that is because the Prosecution has referred to it as "PT2552," and that's the reason why I was under the understanding it had not been entered as an exhibit. If it had been entered as an exhibit, we'd have heard the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour? It was pre-trial exhibit 2152, and, yes, it has been entered as an Exhibit number 77.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that clarification. As I say, Your Honour, I understood it was a pre-trial exhibit being arranged for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Robson. On the original, it does look like the date has been tampered with. On the English version, a particular date is given. I don't know what to make of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it is as you say, that the original version does appear to have had the date altered. It's in evidence. It will be a matter for you in due course to decide what weight you attach the document. I'll also mention this document with the witness in cross-examination as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Robson. You are to carry on, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like the usher to please show the witness what has been marked as P02880 [Realtime transcript read in error "P0880"], and I don't believe this has been entered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me understand one thing, Madam Sartorio. You said "P0880" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- 2880, and then the transcript says "PT." Do you make a distinction between "PT" and "P"?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour. Your Honour, my case manager informs me that in e-court they are called "P0," and she has asked me to use that designation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And not "PT"?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But it's the same document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'd like you to take a look at this document; and if you can, could you please tell us what believe this document to be?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I've never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us what -- okay. Could you look at the second page of the document? Can you find any identifying information on this page?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't. I've never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Would you turn to the third page of the document and see if you can find any identification information.

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can hardly see anything here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are foreigners. I am not sure if I can recognise anyone, and I have never seen this document before. This is an unknown document to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us what it says up in the upper left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says "Number, List of Members of the El Mujahedin Detachment." Is this what you are talking about? Is this what you're asking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. And also who is the document from? What does it say up in the upper left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, "Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Military Post Code 5023." I've never seen this document before. This is the first time that I see a list of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And what is the date on the document?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 26th of February, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the title of the document is?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't really say here, as far as I can see, the title.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, just before the list begins, there is -- there are some words. Could you tell us what those words say?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where? Fine. "List of Members of the El Mujahedin Detachment, Military Post Code 5689, Zenica."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could the Court usher please put the corresponding page to the page on the right, the English? Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, I would like you to look through this document to see whether you can identify whether your name is in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: You're going to have to scroll the document's alphabetical.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is not here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, the court usher needs to please scroll several pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will the witness see when we scroll that fast?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is not here on this list.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'd like the usher to continue to scroll, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could he go a bit slower? Could we maybe scroll up a little bit? Yeah. No. Go slow. Go slow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could the usher zoom in on the top half of this list, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To wait for Alic, Hasib, father's name Mustafa. My name is here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And could you tell us if your dates of service are correct in the right-hand columns?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 15th of May, 1993, 27th of December, 1995. Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit number 97.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, are you receiving a disability pension for your military service in the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not so far. I did receive it for May, but that's not any kind disability benefit. I don't get any kind of disability benefit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Are you receiving a type of pension based on your military service?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got it for May of this year now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Is that the first monetary amount of pension that you have received since your service ended in 1995?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you know the dates upon which your pension is based?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really tell you the exact dates. I don't know what dates are on the certificates. I don't know when it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you a question about one of the operations that you told us about on Friday. You told us about the operation in 1993, when you went from Simulje to Borje to Radonjici. The question is: Do you know if any of the members of your unit in May of 1993 conducted any type of operations in Simulje?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. We all went there together. It wasn't the case that somebody did something individually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second, sir. Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got to raise an objection as to that last question. The witness explained about an operation he participated in, last week during his evidence, where he mentioned Simulje. However, it was firmly established, Your Honour, that that operation took place in either July or August of 1993. So my objection, Your Honour, relates to the leading part concerning May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, that was what the witness stated on Friday. I'm asking him a separate question, though, if any operations were conducted in May of 1993. So it's a separate question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the objection was the fact that the reference was made to May in the same part of the question dealing with operations concerning Simulje. It's line 18 of the transcript, and 19. Your Honour, if my learned friend wishes to establish from scratch that operations took place in May, then that could be legitimate, but not in the same turn of phrase as the operations concerning Simulje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, not in relation to the operation that was referred to last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That's fair, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, a separate question, quite apart from the operation that you described that happened in around July of 1993, I'm asking if prior to that operation, there were any operations conducted in Simulje, particularly in May.

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you know if your unit or any accompanying units with you had to conduct any type of reconnaissance in that area prior to your July operation?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really tell you that. I don't know. Since we knew the ground there, we knew the terrain, and there was not so much need to do any reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, since the war ended in 1995, have you kept in contact with any foreign members of the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. With some of them who got the citizenship, who live there, who have their families, I was in touch with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And do you still see some of them today?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Sartorio. Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Alic. My name is Nicholas Robson. I'll be asking you some questions this morning. You told us last week that you're from Suhi Dol village in Travnik Municipality. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And before the war, you worked there as a farmer; is that so?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it's right to say that in that part of Travnik Municipality, many of the local people were involved in agriculture or raising cattle as their employment?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about the events at the start of the war. Is it right that in April 1992, the Serb forces entered the Travnik region and took up positions on Mount Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And Mount Vlasic is the large mountain above your village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And at the time that the Serb forces arrived, men from the local Bosnian Muslim villages and the Bosnian Croat villages formed village defence units and set up defence lines against the Serbs on Mount Vlasic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know about us. I don't know about Croats, but probably they also did the same thing. They also had those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You can confirm that in the local Bosnian Muslim villages, the men set up defence lines against the Serbs on the mountain?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it was at that time in April 1992 that you believe you effectively joined the Bosnian Army?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, concerning the conditions for the men in the village defence units, the Muslim village defence units, they were bad, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Most of the men were dressed in ordinary civilian clothing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And is it correct that, at that stage, you yourself didn't have a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, right at the beginning, I didn't have a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Also, most of the men didn't have proper military equipment or weapons, did they?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And so they had to make due with hunting rifles or what other weapons they could find; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Also amongst those village defence units, it's right that there were very few men with professional military experience and training; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, that would be the case. Nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And do you agree that the Serbs on Mount Vlasic were much more organised and had better equipment than you in the other villages?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had everything. We had nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, at some point in time, the 306th Mountain Brigade was formed, and you and the other members of the village defence units became part of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And can you confirm, when you and the other men became part of that brigade, conditions did not become better, did they?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Conditions were bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So the members of the 306th Mountain Brigade still did not have weapons or uniforms; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that year, while I was in the army, the situation was completely bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And also once you became a member of the 306th Mountain Brigade, that particular unit still lacked organisation, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there wasn't any organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Turning to 1993, it's right, isn't it, that relations between the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats deteriorated? Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And do you remember, by April 1993, is it right that the Croatian Defence Council had set up roadblocks throughout the area, which made it very difficult for the Bosnian Muslims to travel around?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, last week in your evidence, you told the Court that you left the 306th Mountain Brigade in May 1993. However, at that time, do you remember, it's right that the Bosnian Croats had withdrawn from the defensive positions on Mount Vlasic, facing the Serbs; and at that time, only the Muslims were left defending those lines. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It is possible that the Croats paired up with the Muslims [as interpreted]. It is possible. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just to correct, then, Mr. Alic, what you said, it's possible that the Croats paired up with the Serbs; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, but it doesn't have to be that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In your evidence, you told us that in May 1993, you joined the El Mujahed Detachment. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And when you joined that group of Arab Mujahedin, the number of people in that group was very small, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, can I suggest to you that while it's correct that you joined a group of Arab Mujahedin, it didn't have the name El Mujahed Detachment at that point in time, did it?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it didn't. That's what the villagers later on referred to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You say "later on referred to it." Would you agree with me that the El Mujahed Detachment only -- I should say the group of Arab Mujahedin only became known as the El Mujahed Detachment in August 1993?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, thereabouts, I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, the whole time that you were in the El Mujahed Detachment, it's right, isn't it, that at no time did the Arabs tell you their real names?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they didn't. They all had nicknames.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that they didn't want to reveal their true identities?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, you told us that the group of Mujahedin was located in the village of Poljanice in three Serb houses. Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: After you joined that group, it's correct, isn't it, that the Arab members of the group was constantly changing; and by that I mean, the Arabs were often leaving while others were joining? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could agree to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And after joining that group, it's right to say, isn't it, that combat instructions were issued to members of the group only by the emir of that group?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, emir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that you and the other Mujahedin members would only respond to the command of the emir?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, can you help us with this? In Central Bosnia, around that time in 1993, it's right that there were other Arab groups around, apart from the group that you joined; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, but I don't know. It is possible that there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Again, if you don't know, please say so, but do you recall other Arab groups being in Tesanj?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that. I don't know the answer to that. It is possible that there were, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: That's fine. How about Zepce?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zepce? I don't know that there were any there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alic, I'd like to show you a document. It's Exhibit 67. It was admitted into evidence last week. Whilst we're waiting for that document to appear on the screens, if I could just ask you: It's right, isn't it, you told us in your evidence last week that you became a member of the Bosnian Army from 4th of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps, if we could just look at the next page in both the B/C/S and English version, just to verify what the main front page of this document is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So we can see it's a document headed, "Overview of the El Mujahedin Detachment." The page I'm interested in is page 4 in both the English and the B/C/S versions.

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. I beg your pardon. It's page 3 of the B/C/S version that we're interested in, and it's page 4 of the -- it should be page 4 of the English translation. But perhaps if we can just pull up the corresponding page. Your Honour, we're still waiting for the corresponding page. It should be the page before this one on the document. Your Honour, I believe I should be able to deal with this point on the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alic, if we look at the list and if we go down to number 4, we can see your name there, can't we, "Alic, Hasib"?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, if we look across the document and look at the third column, we can see a heading at the top of that third column. Do you see that heading?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A list of members of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. And if we go below that, what I'm interested in is the -- in the third column along, do you see where it says at the top of that third column: "In Army of BiH as of ..."? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the BH Army from a certain date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Exactly. So what it says is or what the meaning is, the person was in the BiH Army from a certain date. Now, if we go down --

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we go down the list to your entry, under Point number 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: -- is it correct that you were in the Bosnian Army from the 15th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th, I joined the detachment; and up to the 14th, I was in the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So where this document states that you were in the Army of BiH as from May 1993, does that mean that this information is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that I was with the El Mujahed Detachment as of the 15th of May, 1993. This list doesn't show that I was a member of the army at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, I think the question that I'm asking you is that at the top of the column, it says: "In Army of BiH as of ..." In other words, date commencing in the Bosnian Army, and it has a date stated here, "15th of May, 1993." It's right, isn't it, that from what you told us earlier, you actually commenced service in the Bosnian Army in April 1992; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to refer you to another document. This is Exhibit 78. This is the -- this is a military record that was referred to last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps, if we could initially look at page 1 of this document, the first page containing -- the particular page that we're interested in is -- I'll give you the ERN number. It's 0365-5060.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson, we have been given a hard copy of this document. Do you want to carry on?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you have the hard copy, that's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Except that I'm not able to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, copies of a translation have been provided as well, so the court usher should be able to give you a hard copy of the B/C/S and English versions of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, could -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Does Your Honour have both versions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, can I just confirm that you have got a B/C/S document in front of you, a two-page document; and on the first page, up in the top left-hand corner at number 1, it has your name, "Alic, Mustafa Hasib"?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you remember being shown this document last week by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If you could turn over onto the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, the English translation does not exactly correspond to the B/C/S version, so it's page 4 of the English translation we're interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alic, you were asked questions about your military service last week. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I can refer your attention to Point 33 on the this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can -- Your Honour, I see we now have it up on our screen as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that Point 33 has a heading that states "Promotions." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In front of you, do you see the part of the document - it's in Box number 33 - and it should say "Promotions"? It's the second page of the document.

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it: "Private sergeant" and "First sergeant."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I realise you're looking at both pages, so I realise it's probably me that's confusing you as well. So I apologise for that. So let's focus our attention on the left-hand side of this document, first of all. In your evidence, as I understand it, you were a common soldier in the Bosnian Army. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And then when you joined the group of Mujahedin that went on to be called the El Mujahed Detachment, it's correct, isn't it, that you remained a common soldier; is that so?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, in this left-hand -- on this left-hand side of the document, in Box 33, "Promotions," it states a number of positions, doesn't it? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So it states that for you, first of all, you were "razvodnik"?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree that you were a razvodnik, a private?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, if we go on to the next entry, it states "Sergeant." You were never a sergeant, were you?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we go along that part of the document, Point 2, "Sergeant," we can see a date there at the end, "Pro/E datum," 1994. If we go down to the next entry, Point number 3, it states for you -- it states: "First sergeant." It's right, you were never a first sergeant, were you?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never a first sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. And now I'd like to refer you to the date on this particular document, which is at the bottom of the same page on the left-hand side. This is at page 5 in the English translation. It's right, isn't it, Mr. Alic, that this document, which supposedly sets out your military history, is stamped and dated 19th of January 1988? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So this document was signed and dated more than three years before you actually joined the Bosnian Army; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, I'd now like to refer you to another exhibit. It's a photograph that we looked at last week. It's Exhibit 96, and it's Photograph number 4 of the tents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, for the record, I'm just going to specify that this document is ERN 0292-3920. Now, last week, when you were asked about this photograph by the Prosecutor, you said: "As far as I can make out, this is the 13th kilometre where we were located." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: First of all, would you agree with me that this is not a particularly good-quality photograph?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's nothing special, but there you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what we can see here are simple tents that you would have been able to see in many places around Bosnia at that time; is that so?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And the Bosnian Army used these sorts of tents throughout the country during the war, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me there's nothing particularly special about the scenery, is there? We can see a lot of trees, but this particular place could be almost anywhere or many places in Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could be anywhere; but as I've told you, this could be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that, when we look at the photograph, there are no special features that could identify it as the 13th kilometre? We don't see any mountains, for example?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is some hills -- hills around, but the photo is not very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And last week in your evidence, you mentioned there were two or three abandoned buildings at the 13th kilometre. We can't see them in this photograph, can we?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And there's nothing in particular to tell us what year the photograph was taken, is there?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when this was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So would you agree with me when I say that we can't be certain that this is a picture of the 13th-kilometre location?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be any other place; but as far as I know, this should be the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just one moment, Your Honour. Your Honour, those complete -- that completes my questions. But before I sit down, I'd just like to ask that the translation of the last document, P76, be admitted into evidence -- 78, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As I understand it, the Bosnian version was admitted into evidence last week, but we didn't have an English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Well, may the translation of Exhibit 78 please be admitted into evidence. I guess it's going to be given the same number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. I've been informed that apparently, when the Prosecution document was admitted into evidence, it's a substantial document containing many, many, many pages. So I think just for the purpose of keeping this particular document clear, it would be useful if we admitted both the English translation and that page together as a separate document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So be it. Then, these pages of the Bosnian version, together with the English translation thereof, may they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit number 98.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We have no redirect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Judge, no questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, thank you very much. That concludes your testimony in the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That completes your testimony, as I was still saying. Thank you very much for coming; and on behalf of the Tribunal, I just want to say thank you for availing yourself as a witness in this matter. You are now excused. You may stand down. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio. Mr. Mundis is standing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The next witness the Prosecution calls is Saban Alic. I will indicate that I am not sure if this witness is yet in the building. We had anticipated that the cross-examination might have required a little bit more time. Perhaps, with the Trial Chamber's indulgence, we could take the first break at this point in time, and I can assure you that he will definitely be here at 10.30 to commence his direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If we take our break now and come back at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court adjourns and comes back at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis. A new witness. Okay. May the witness make the declaration. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Alic.

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court your name, spelling of your first and last name?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: My name is Saban Alic; A-l-i-c, S-a-b-a-n.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: 11th of December, 1969.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Where were you born, sir?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Suhi Dol in the Travnik Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Were you living in Suhi Dol in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Court, when did the war begin in your area? When did it begin in your area?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, the armed conflict itself in our area started only in 1993; but in 1992, a line was set up against the Serbs in the Vlasic area; the Territorial Defence, as it was at the time. It was actually organised village by village on the initiative of the local people, and the line was set up, up there on Mount Vlasic. It wasn't much of a line, but we, in my village, Suhi Dol, we had a dugout where we took it in shifts. We'd stay up there for 48 hours, and then your turn would come again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Just to confirm, then, you were a member of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the very first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what was the very first day?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you the exact date. It was in the spring of 1992. I don't really know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: How far is Vlasic from your village of Suhi Dol?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, in terms of kilometres, you can only walk there, and it would take you maybe two or two and a half hours to get there on foot, from the village to the place where we held this position in this dugout.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And who was on the other side of your lines in 1992 on Mount Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, the Serbs. They held the communication relay at Vlasic. It was called Paljenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Where, precisely on that line, were you assigned when you were with the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, I and we who held this position there, it was at Vlasicka Gromila, the Vlasic summit on our side, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And who was your commander when you were in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yeah. It's been a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I understand, sir. When you went to the line, you mentioned that you went in shifts to the line. What precisely did you do when you were there?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Up there, while we were up there in the dugouts, well, we had an observation post set up there that looked on to Paljenik, and we took shifts there in pairs. We would stay there for two hours and we would observe in this direction, and that was our task, the task that we carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Sir, if you added up all the people who were manning all of those shifts, how many people would that have been?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps a dozen, 12, something like that. Fifteen, ten to 15, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you remain in the Territorial Defence throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I was in the Territorial Defence up until the time when the 306th Brigade was set up in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you then become a member of the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And who was your commander in the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I forgot his name. I know the man, but I don't know his -- I can't remember his name anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of any commanders you had in the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I remember the commander of my company. That was Sinan Begovic. And I didn't spend that much time there, and I really wasn't interested in it all that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You said the commander of your company was Sinan Begovic. How big was the company?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe 30 of us were in this company. We had a dugout that we held at Ljuta Greda. The company was designated as an anti-armour company. And according to the establishment, that's what it was, an armour company, but we didn't have any anti-armour weapons at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So what was, then, the military objective, as you understood it, of being stationed at Ljuta Greda?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, the objective was to hold the line, to defend all those areas that Serbs had not taken up until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So, at the dugout at Ljuta Greda, how many people would be on each shift?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, five or six of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how often would you do a shift?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, there wasn't much of an organisation there. Often, it would happen to me, or to my group, that when we arrived there, some soldiers, if I may call them that, would already be there in our dugout. So we didn't have -- there was not enough room for us there, and we would just turn around and go back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you remain in the 306th Brigade throughout the rest of the war?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: No. On the 1st of June, 1993, I went to Zapode. There was a group of Arabs there, and I transferred to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: This might be an appropriate time to have the witness shown, in the map book, particularly Map 9, which is marked 0618-6704.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you see a map in front of you, sir, on the screen?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness can be handed a pen so that he can -- or be shown how to mark this electronically.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, looking at this map, could you please make a mark where Zapode is located?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately, somewhere here, maybe 300 or 400 metres from Mehurici, in the direction of Poljanice. It's a straight line.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And just for the record, if you could put a "1" next to that mark, so that later, when we're looking at the record, we will know what it is you indicated.

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, when -- on June 1st, 1993, when you joined this group at Zapode, was the 306th Brigade still maintaining the line at Ljuta Greda?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And when you went to Zapode, did you tell your commander, Sinan Begovic, that you were leaving?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't say anything to anyone. I just went away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you fill out any paperwork in order to leave the 306th and go to this group?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely nothing. A friend of mine had already gone there and he came to my home to pick me up, and I just went with him. There was no paperwork. I didn't say anything to anyone, and nobody actually asked me anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Why did you decide to go to the group at Zapode?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, the very fact that, according to the establishment, the dugout at Ljuta Greda belonged to us; and then we would go there and somebody was already there, and they would say, "No, no. It's not yours." There was a lot of disorder, lack of discipline, and the main reason that prompted me was religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you go to the group at Zapode to avoid military service?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: No, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you consider yourself to be leaving the ABiH when you went to the group at Zapode?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, the way I saw things, at that time, the way I understood things, for as long as you held a rifle and for as long as there was danger for our families and for our survival, I could not consider myself having left the ranks. I consider myself to still belong to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: At what time did you arrive at Zapode on June 1st, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Around noon. I remember that it was lunch when we got there, and we joined them for lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: How many people were there?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, not many of them. Maybe about ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you recall any of their names?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, I know Abu Minah, the cook. His name stuck in my memory. I remember Dzafer. He was also an Arab. Then Abu Bada [phoen], at least that's what we called him. I don't know what his real name was; there was also Abu Haris. I don't really recall right now who was there at the time. There were some people that I was not introduced to, and I never was introduced to them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So you're mentioning names. Were they primarily Arabs that were at Zapode?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the time when I got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions about the camp at Zapode. Could you please describe what it looked like?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: The camp is maybe 300 or 400 metres away from Mehurici, as I already said. There were three houses there. They all belonged to Serbs. It is not a flat area. There is a slight slope. There are some woods separating one house from the rest of the houses. There was the -- the third house was further away, hidden by some woods. There were some fruit trees, but mostly it was a grassy area. It was not tilled. The land was not tilled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Were there Serbs living in the house when you went there in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: No. The houses had already been taken. I don't know what happened to those Serbs. I didn't know them at all, not even from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You mentioned the camp was 300 or 400 metres from Mehurici. Did you see any other military units in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: At that time or later on?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: At that time.

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, sometime before that - I don't know how long before that - Jajce fell into the Serb hands. So quite a few of those - I don't know what their unit was called - but there were quite a few of those people in Mehurici. We called them "Krajisnici," the people from Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You mentioned that you came to Zapode with a friend. Did he remain with you there throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: No. This friend of mine got wounded quite soon after this. He was hit by shrapnel in his eye, and soon he left and he went abroad to get treatment. And he lives in Finland to this day. He hasn't come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: How soon after you came to Zapode was the action that resulted in his injury?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe a week, seven or eight days, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Between the time you came to Zapode and that military action, did you leave the camp?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: No, not at all. I didn't leave the camp, not even to go back home. I spent the entire time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you notice other people camped at Zapode leave the camp?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, a long time has passed. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Who is the commander of the camp at that time?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: The commander of the camp was Abu Haris.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness a photograph, but I would like to keep this -- the map that he's already marked, I'd like to keep it, if that's possible. I see that it's not. So I'll stick with the map and have him mark that, and move on to the next thing after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, I want to ask you some questions now about the military operation that you said resulted in the injury of your friend. Did you also participate in that military operation?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Had you ever participated in actual combat before that?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Up until that time, no. That was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: When did you first find out that you were going to engage in combat?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I found that out on the eve of this action. The night before, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how did you find out?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, on the eve of the action, some groups were set up. People were assigned to groups, and there was a call for volunteers. And only those people who wanted to go into this action, to r to break through the lines, they were put into those groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And who assigned people to the groups?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: When people volunteered, then there was Vahidin and Muatez, and there were some other people I didn't get to know all that well. I didn't know at the time that those were their names. I learned it later, although I was with them there. I lived with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You mention Abu Haris was the commander of the camp. Was he involved in assigning people to the groups?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And you mention a person named Muatez. Was he also involved with that?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Abu Haris wasn't. Abu Haris had other duties, as far as I could see, but Muatez was a soldier and he was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you know what other duties Abu Haris had?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I know that he was a medical doctor by profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So I want to ask you some questions now about the day of the operation itself. At what point did you leave the camp at Zapode?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I was not in that break-through group that was to launch the attack, somewhere between Suhi Dol and Poljanice. I followed the group. It was at dawn. It was already daylight. I don't know how late it could have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I believe the map is still in front of you, sir.

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And I see that you have the pen in your hand.

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could you please mark on the map where it is that you're talking about, when you said you went to a place between Suhi Dol and Poljanice or Zapode?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: This would be somewhere around here, approximately. [Marks] There are a lot of paths that the villagers used to reach the fields. We took one of those paths.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And, sir, if I could please have you place the number "2" next to that mark, so that later we'll be able to determine what it is you've indicated there.

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You said you weren't in the group that was doing the spearheading. How many people were in that group, that first group?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: They left when it was still dark, so it's very difficult for me to say how many of them went. I wouldn't know their exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: How many people were in your group?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Between ten and 15. Not that many.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any of the people in that group?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I know from the village of Dub, his name was Fusko Ramo; Zuhdija Sehic, my friend, was with us. There were some other people whose names I can't remember at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: How long did it take you to get from Zapode, which is number 1 on the map, to what's been marked number 2 on the map?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Maybe between 20 to 30 minutes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And by the time you got to number 2, the position marked number 2, did you see the first group that went out ahead of you?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: No, I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Okay. So, after you arrived at the position on the map marked number 2, how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: We did not stop there. The line had already been broken through, so we followed immediately after the first group. There was a clearing there. We ran, in the direction of Simulje, we ran across that clearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And, sir, if you could, if you could mark on the map where Simulje is located.

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And if you could put a number "3" next to that.

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how long did it take you to get to that position, if you recall, sir?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Maybe 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: How did you know to run in that direction towards Simulje?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew because my village, Suhi Dol, is below, and I had used to come to Simulje even before. This is where we played football. I'm very well acquainted with Simulje, and I was at the time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: But how did you know on that day, during that military operation, that you were to run in the direction of Simulje?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Even before the operation, I arrived there. The Croats had set up the lines; and from my village, while I was still not in Zapode, I would come to that line. That's how I knew where they were. Our villagers manned a line below Simulje on the border of that level field.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, generally where the Croat lines were?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, the Croat lines were on a slope. I can't see it on the screen. It's not depicted on this map. In any case, as you come from the direction of Simulje, and as you reach that slope, below it, in the direction of Radonjici and Maline, there is a steep slope. It was some sort of a long elevation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could you mark that front line on that map, sir? I understand you might not be able to determine the topography, but could you mark generally where the line was?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: This is the clearing from Simulje leading upwards. That's the only thing that looks like it. Here somewhere, it was. [Indicates] I can't be any more precise; although, I'm familiar with the area. I had been there before. I went there after this operation. A path leads through here up to the mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So could you mark on the map, sir, draw the line where the Bosnian Croat line was?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: It was here in Percin. [Indicates] I know that they were up there in Percin. They had a dugout there, and then in the direction above Gornje Maline, and then towards Postinje. As you follow the edge between Gornje and Donje Maline, the line continued all the way up to Mount Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I see, sir, there are two marks on the map. Could you please draw a line where you're talking about where the line was, the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: It says "Percin" here, and I know that the line was here, and then it gets somewhat less clear. But in any case, it was above Maline, Gornje, and Donje Maline. This is where the line was, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could you indicate that line on the map, sir?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: There's something I'm not very clear about here. There's something that is confusing here. The line was somewhere in Bikosi as you go towards Postinje, but there was also above Maline, above Gornje, and Donje Maline. I'm afraid I can't find my bearings on this map. It's rather difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I notice that there are three dots on the map, at least three -- I guess four dots on the map. Those appear in blue.

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Those points indicate where positions are on the Bosnian Croat line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure. I'm 100 per cent sure about Percin. The rest, I'm afraid I'm not sure. The picture is not the one that I'm familiar with. I cannot tally what I have in my head and what I see on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Okay. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've indicated some positions there. On the day of the operation, how did you know that you were to head towards Simulje and not, for instance, towards Percin or toward Bikosi?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, I was with the group. I was maybe the fifth or the sixth in the group, and I just followed the others, those who were in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you recall who was in charge of your group?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm a bit confused about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Who told you to go to what's been marked as Point 2 on the map in the morning?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you, we left Zapode in a group, single file. I followed the others. Nobody said, "March," actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You said before that you ran from Point 2 to Point 3, and where did you run to?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I didn't say that. I ran from Simulje - hold on just a moment - across Simulje. We ran across Simulje, because that was a clearing, and there was a possibility that somebody could have stayed behind and that they could have intercepted us. From Point 2 to Point 3, this is where we ran across through that area, from Simulje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: After you got to Simulje, where did you run to, sir? Where did you go? Where did you proceed to?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: We crossed Simulje and we came to their trenches, to their line. I saw one or two dead bodies in the trench, and then we proceeded towards Borovi. I don't know how they are depicted here on the map, but in any case we called that location "Borovi."

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could you mark where Borje is on the map, sir?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Borovi is above Radonjici. Maybe this is it. [Indicates] I would say that this is that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I see that Borje is marked in blue. Could you please put a number "4" next to that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Also, sir, if you could please indicate where it was that you saw the bodies in the trench.

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: On the line, the line leading from Percin downwards and ended above Donje Maline. I was talking about that slope. As you cross that slope, this is where they were. And they were not dugouts; they were trenches. I remember that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I see you've put a mark on this map right before where the "G" for "Gornje Maline" is. Could you please mark that as "5," so we can distinguish it from the other marks you've put on the page?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, did you stop at -- it might be better to clarify something here first. Could you please spell "Borje"?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether this is Borje. It says "Borje" here, but we called that area Borovi, because there are a lot of pine trees there. That's why we called the area "Borovi."

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Do you stay in this area?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And for how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Maybe an hour. One of our men had gotten killed here. There was a tent here. I wasn't in that tent. The Croats were billeted there in that tent. Our men entered that tent to take some rest. However, one of the Croats, not knowing that it was our men in the tent, arrived and said, "Good morning." And when he realised that he was not talking to his own men, he opened a burst of fire on our man, killing one of our soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And I want to clarify for the record, sir. When you say "Croats," are you referring to Croats or Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Bosnian Croats, of course. I suppose they were Bosnian Croats. Maybe there was somebody else from somewhere else. In any case, they were wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: After Borje, where did you proceed to, sir?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I went down to the village of Radonjici.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could you indicate Radonjici on the map?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And please put a number "6" by Radonjici?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Radonjici that day?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Not long. Since the Croats had carried out an operation at Bandol, my group proceeded to go down to Bandol, where my friend actually got wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could you please mark Bandol on this map and put a number "7" by it?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. So you said your group proceeded to Bandol. Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Somebody was looking for a local who would be familiar with the terrain, and somebody pointed to me and said I was local. And Muatez was to go back to Zapode. I didn't know why. I didn't know at the time his name was Muatez. I returned from Radonjici to Zapode, together with Muatez.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what route did you follow, sir?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: We went back to Borovi; and from Borovi, we followed their line downwards across Bikosi, and then we arrived in Zapode.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And why was it that you followed their line?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: It was the safest route. There were no mines, landmines there, so we opted for that for safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If you could, sir, please draw a line along the route that you followed between Radonjici and Zapode.

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Again, I am confused. I'm just not able to get my bearings. This place, Borje, and the line --

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask another way. Did you -- did you pass through Bikosi?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you pass through --

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: There is an asphalt road. As you follow this line along the slope, there is something like a ridge; and following the top of that ridge, you go down to Bikosi. And there is one segment of asphalt; and as you follow that, you enter Zapode.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did this route take you through Maline?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: No. Maline is to the right. If you were to go through Maline, you would prolong the whole journey. So, no, you can't. You can't go that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: At what time did you pass through Bikosi?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to remember exactly. I don't know. Maybe 12:00, or half past 11.00, maybe. I know that we arrived around noon or before the noon, because we went to the mosque to say our prayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: When you say you arrived around noon or before noon, to what location are you referring? Where did you arrive to?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: In Zapode. We reached our destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And who were you with?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: With Muatez.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Were you with anybody else?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Just the two of us. Our order, or my order, was to take him to Zapode. I was to escort him because he was not familiar with the terrain. That was our destination, Zapode.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How did you travel, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On foot, of course. You could not even use the car there because of the configuration of the ground. There's just a foot path, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you said there's an asphalt road somewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There is some asphalt, maybe 300 to 400 metres, but only through Bikosi. As you descend from that ridge, you can only take that foot path. As you come to the village, maybe there is 200 or 300 metres of asphalt road, maybe not even that much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If I could have just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Looking at this map, I'm wondering if you can tell us, just for the sake of the record, showing the numbers, just saying the numbers out loud, what is the route that you followed from Zapode to Radonjici? So, for instance, Zapode is at number 1.

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is no path on this side, just a foot path which people used to reach their farms. If you want to go to Radonjici, you have to go from Krpeljici. There is an asphalt road up to Radonjici from Krpeljici or from Guca Gora. And from Krpeljici, you can get to Radonjici.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Would it be fair, sir, to say, based on what your testimony is today, that you followed this route to Radonjici on that day, from Position 1 to Position 2 to Position 3, which is Borje, to Position -- and Position 3 is Simulje - I'm sorry - to Position 4, which is Borje, and then to 6, which is Radonjici? So it would be 1, 2, 3, 4, 6; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I would like to object. On two occasions, the witness has expressed his doubts about the location of Borje. He is speaking about Borovi, and he's being suggested that the place is called Borje, although he has mentioned Borovi on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought, Madam Vidovic, that at some stage, he said they called it Borovi, although it is called Borje. Let's just see if we can find that part. And I do remember Mr. Wood saying, "I thank you for that clarification," after that. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is not the way I understood it, but maybe the witness can be asked to clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that in the map it says "Borje."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Wood, would you like to clear that point with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: When you refer to the place called Borovi, Mr. Alic, is that place represented by number 4 on the map?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly. I said, "if that's it." If Borje is this place, Borovi, then that's what it is. It's difficult for me to really figure it out on this map. We called it "Borovi," and that means pine trees, because there were many pine trees there. It is somewhere there. All of it is there in the vicinity. I know you can see Krpeljici from there. It is close to Radonjici. You can see Radonjici and Guca Gora, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, Madam Vidovic, if you'd look at also page 41 from line 22 into page 42, you'll see a similar explanation given there. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, precisely. This is the reason why I raise this objection, because, Your Honour, it doesn't follow from this that this is one and the same location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, he says, "It says 'Borje' here, but we called that area Borovi." That's his testimony. I don't know whether you can take it much further than that. If you want to say did he say Borje and there is a Borovi, which are two different places, fine, then we'll hear from you when you show us those two places. However, his testimony is that what is called "Borje" on the map is what they call "Borovi" because there are lots of pine trees there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
