utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will clear this up with the witness in my cross-examination, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Alic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just ask for a point of clarification, because I'm not sure of where all of this is taking us in relation to the indictment. What is the relevance of all these movements during these days?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think that will be clear with a few more questions I'll ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I certainly hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess you may proceed, because Madam Vidovic says she will clear this up with the witness when she cross-examines.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Getting to the Judge's question, then, Mr. Alic. Did you engage in any other combat operations in this area during the time you were with the El Mujahed Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: The El Mujahed Detachment was set up later, and it was given this designation. Before that, it was just called "The Arabs," and people would say, "He's gone to join the Arabs." That's what the people would say. That's what the group was called; and then the El Mujahed Detachment was established, but this was later on. Yeah. We had -- we had such actions. We called them --

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If I could interrupt, sir. After this operation, what was the status of the Bosnian Croats in this area?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, there were no Croats left there. They had been expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Was the HVO defeated in this operation?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And were there any other military operations that you participated in after this time? In this area? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: In this area, specifically, there was no line there, so there was no combat. This area had been cleaned up, and I can't see what other kinds of actions would be -- operations would be required.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And, again, this operation took place in early June 1993?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, getting back to the map, sir. I know I keep asking this question, but I want to try and make sure the record is clear, so that when we're looking at this later, we can see from the transcript, and looking at your map, exactly what route you took. So if you could, please, look at the map and tell the Court what is the order that you followed on your way from Zapode to Radonjici in June 1993. Starting, of course, with Zapode is at number 1, the place where you gathered for the battle is number 2, and then could you tell us, please, where it is you proceed after that by using the numbers?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: We headed out from Zapode. That was in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Zapode is number 1?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Number 1, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And then you proceeded to which position?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: The location marked with "2." It's not -- it doesn't have a name. It's further down from Simulje. And from there, we headed towards Simulje. So those were our lines further below from Simulje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And Simulje is marked number 3?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, I think this is where there might be confusion on the record. Number 5 is where you saw the bodies, you testified; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Above Simulje, the bodies were on the line in the trench, just lying there in the trench. As I crossed the line that day that they held, I saw two or three bodies just lying there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And that is at number 5; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I don't know what we marked with number 5. But at the line at the top of Simulje, at the ridge there, that's where the line was and that should be number 5. Now, I don't know what we marked with number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And after that, you proceeded to Borje -- well, the position marked number 4 on the map; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Towards Borovi. I keep saying "Borovi," but if Borje and Borovi is the same, then I agree with you. But given it's the same, we headed towards Borovi. It says here "Borje." Now, I can't really tell you if it's one and the same thing. Perhaps there's another location called Borje which is not the same as Borovi, so I always put in this caveat, if that Borje and Borovi are the same. So we headed towards this hill. I don't know whether Borje and Borovi are one in the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: This hill is marked number 4. The place where you proceeded next is marked number 4; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: After that, you proceeded to what's been marked number 6; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what's been marked number 7 is where the rest of your group went, that's Bandol, but you did not go to number 7; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you could -- the reason I wanted to clear this up is I wonder if you could show us the route you took to go -- to return to Zapode; that is, to show us on the map?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I can't do it here because I can't do it precisely enough. I went back following their line, which was along the ridge above Simulje. This is where their line was, and we took this slope from this ridge towards Bikosi. We followed in their footsteps, so to speak. We went to Bikosi, and then we went west from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say you followed their line, whose line did you follow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The line that they held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who are the "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Croats. Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But I thought --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But I thought the line you showed us that you thought the Croats held ran in an east-west direction, and you were travelling south-north. Going back to Zapode from Radonjici, you travel south-north. But I thought when you indicated the line held by the Croats, if you look at the blue dots on the map that you made, they run in a -- what is that? That is vertical? What is that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Horizontal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Horizontal. In a horizontal line from the west to the east.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I cannot collate what is in my head and what is on the map, because the vision of the terrain that I have in my head. And I'm really very familiar with it, I was born there, I know it inside out. And now I can't find my way around on this map to compare it to what -- the image that I have in my head of the situation on the terrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that, sir. Forget about the map. Let's look at the image in your head. The image in your head showed the line that was held by the Croats to be running in a horizontal plane from the west to the east; and according to the image that you are trying to explain to us, going back from Radonjici to Zapode, you go south-north. So you can't follow the line of the Croats because you are going to cross it. Irrespective of whether this in this area or in The Hague here, you are going to go across that line. You are not following that line, and that's what I'm not understanding. That's why I'm asking you to clear me on that one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is how I can explain: We were at Radonjici. We pick up Muatez. We went back to Borje. We went back to their lines, so we're going back towards Simulje. So we're not taking the same route that we took on our way there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You went back to their line. You did not follow their line. That's something different. Thank you very much. Thank you for that clarification. You may proceed, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: After you returned to Zapode, how long did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: We spent the night there; and in the morning, we went back to Radonjici again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And during your time in Zapode, before you returned to Radonjici, did you ever have occasion to leave the camp at all?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I didn't go out at all. I was there. I didn't go out at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you recall who was in the camp at that time with you, other than Muatez, obviously?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I remember this Abdu Rahman Yemeni who was interpreting at the prayer, and I remember that he cried at this rite, and that's how I remember him. I was touched by that. There were not many of us there, just a few, at least not in the house where I was, because there were three houses. It's possible that there were some other people in those other houses. But in the house where I was, there weren't that many of us, seven or eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'd like to have the map captured and admitted into evidence, Your Honour, or tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The map on the screen is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number 99.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I see that it's nearly noon. This might be an appropriate time for a break, at least in terms of the flow of the direct examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We're going on until noon, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you done with the examination? We're going up to noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes. We started at 10.30, and it's been an hour and 15 minutes. That's the only reason I bring it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. But because of when we took our first break, we will go up to noon. I guess the tapes can take us there. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Then I'll proceed. I'm happy to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: While you were at Zapode, did you see any -- anybody pass by on the road outside going in the direction of Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, in that house where I was, there is a wooded area dividing this house from the other one, and I was also inside. So I couldn't really see anything, nor, to tell you the truth, did I pay any attention. People would walk down that road. This is the road that led to Poljanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I want to ask a quick follow-up question about the group that you were in during the operation itself. Can you tell us the composition of that group? Were you the only person from Bosnia in that group?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I said that Ramo Fusko was there, and Zuhdija, this friend of mine. There were some others there. It was a long time ago, so I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Were there any Arabs in your group on that day?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Maybe two or three in my group.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Sir, I want to also ask you some other questions about other members who were in that area. Did you know a person named Ishak Aganovic?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps interpreter didn't pronounce the name as you pronounced it. His name is Isak Aganovic, not Ishak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, sir. Was this Aganovic a member of the group you were in? And let me clarify that. Was he at the camp at Zapode at around the same time?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't really make any claims, because I really don't know. We didn't really know each other. Later on, we got acquainted a little bit; but, at that time, I really didn't know him. I didn't socialise with him, so I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: But was he a member of that group, the group that would become the El Mujahed Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I know that he was a driver in our detachment. He'd drive us to the line and back, but I really don't know. I can't make any claims. Really, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you remember any occasions when he drove you to the line?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, he drove us there many times. He drove a Bedford truck. We thought he was a good driver, and we always wanted Isak to drive us because it would take us less time to get home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Was this in 1993 or later?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I think it was later, because he was not the driver initially. He didn't drive the truck; and then later on, he learned how to do it. He got some training. I think it was in -- when we were on the other side, the Sejdici and Zavidovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you know where Ishak Aganovic, the person you're referring to as Isak Aganovic, is from?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, he's from Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Sir, did you know a person named Zihnija Sejdic.

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Zihnija Sejdic, yes. He's a relative of mine. I know him very well. I've known him since our childhood. We grew up together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And where is he from, sir?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: He is from Sejdici, so our families are related. And he would often come to our place at Suhi Dol, and I would often visit him at Sejdici.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what municipality is Sejdici in?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: It's just part of Poljanice. That's what it is. Sejdici is part of Poljanice. It's there near Mehurici, a village near Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: This Sejdici, what's his father's name -- I'm sorry, this Zejdic?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: He's dead, Zahid. He's been dead for a long time. His name is Zahid.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And this Sejdic, was he a member of the same unit?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'd see him there. He was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: When did you see him there?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't really say whether this was before the action or after the action. I can't really put a time to it. I would see him there. I think it was mostly after the action, but he was there at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: After you left Zapode, sir, where did you go? I'm talking now about the day of the -- about the operation.

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: On the day of the operation, that morning, is that what you mean? I said. I already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You testified that you came -- you accompanied Muatez from Radonjici to Zapode. You stayed overnight in Zapode. Where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Afterwards, I went back to Radonjici again. So in the morning, a group of us - our emir was Muhamed Basic. That's why we called him emir; it's like a commander - a group of maybe five or six of us who were there, he took us to Radonjici. And we spent seven or eight days up there in Radonjici. We didn't move from there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What route did you take to go from Zapode to Radonjici on that morning, the morning after the operation?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: We took the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You keep referring to the morning after the operation. I'm not quite sure I'm following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The witness testified that the operation -- the day of the operation, he ended in Radonjici, and then he went back to Zapode with Muatez; and then he testified that he stayed overnight in Zapode, and after that, returned to Radonjici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So this is the following day?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The following day, yes. That's how I understood his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wood, for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what route did you take to get back to Radonjici the day after the operation?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: We took the same route that we used during the action. We went to Simulje, and then on to Radonjici and to Borovi, and then we went down to Radonjici.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And that route did not take you to Bikosi; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Not that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I see it is 11.56. This is not a bad time for me to end, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're done with your --

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, I have a few more questions. I'll consult with my colleagues, of course, but I would like to wrap up very quickly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, why don't you wrap up now, actually, so that we can finish your examination-in-chief before the break. And could I remind you also that as far as I can see, you had set aside one hour for examination-in-chief of this witness, and so far we have already spent an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I'm mindful of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I wouldn't want to see you run out of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could have the witness shown Exhibit 67, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If I could draw your attention on that list, sir, to number 72, if we could scroll forward. Do you see number 72, sir?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Is this the person you were speaking of before, this Sejdic?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Zihnija Sejdic. I think it is. 9th of January, 1970. I know that he was born in 1970.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I think at this time the Prosecution has no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Wood. This may then be an appropriate moment to take a break. We'll come back at half past 12.00. Thank you very much. Court is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Alic. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and I will be cross-examining you on behalf of General Rasim Delic's Defence. Very often, you'll be in a position to answer my question by either saying "yes" or "no." If either I or the Trial Chamber do not seek additional clarification, for the sake of saving time, I would kindly ask you by to reply by saying "yes" or "no" whenever possible. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to ask you this: You served in the former JNA, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You served from 1979 for a year?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: From March.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: From March 1989 onwards?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the war started, you joined the Territorial Defence of Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you joined a local unit, a village unit of the Territorial Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You've also explained that after that, you joined the 306th Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I did not join them. Actually, yes, I was a member of the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have mentioned that Mr. Sinan Begovic was the leader of the so-called anti-armour company that you belonged to?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The anti-armour company was just a name; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: It was just its formation. We did not have any anti-armour tools or devices. However, as part of those brigades, that had to exist on paper. Such a company had to exist on paper. There was a company, it had some men, but we did not have any things to use to fight against armoured vehicles or tanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, on paper, sometimes you would find things that did not reflect the reality on the ground?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The army existed as an organised force on TV just to boost the morale. When it came to the reality, the army looked more like village units. Nobody obeyed anybody. There was no authority. It was not a normal, organised military. You had to be a member, because if you refused, the police would be after you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'll go back to the question of the police. Generally speaking, you were not well armed, were you?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: We were very badly armed. We had some hunting rifles in the village, here and there somebody had a pistol. And in our village, there was a military man who had brought two automatic rifles from the army, and that's all we had. When we manned the line, we had some weapons. The weapons were always at the dugout. The shifts would change, the arms would stay there, because people did not have their own weapons. They had to use whatever was available.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. At one point in testifying, you said that you did not even remember who the commander of the 306th Brigade was. Would you agree with me -- would you accept if I told you that, at that time, you didn't even know who the brigade commander was? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I suppose so, because I really didn't know. If I'd known then, maybe I would know now. I suppose I would know now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree with me that towards the end of April 1993, the Croatian Defence Council blocked the area by setting up check-points on all major roads?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: The goal of the operation that we discussed a while ago was to launch a counter-attack against the Croats who had already attacked and killed about eight people, eight of our people in Bukovica. They killed eight and they took away the others. We had to launch an operation in that area. Donje Maline was encircled. The road leading to Zenica from our part did not function. We were under a total blockade. There was just one passible road to Serici and almost to Zenica. We could not go to Travnik. We could not go to Zenica. We could not go to Maline. We had no communication with Donje Maline. We could not go on that road. It was not possible. It was only for horse and carts.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify one thing. At this moment, we are discussing the time when you were a member of the 306th Brigade. Do you understand that? ?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Parts of the brigade, for the reasons you've just specified, could not communicate with each other; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also, part of the brigade could not communicate with the command? Would you know that at all?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We could not communicate, or the communication was rather difficult. All of these hamlets, all of these villages, were separated by various check-points. There were obstacles, and it was not possible to go from one village to another. We could not communicate. We were all under our separate blockade. The blockade was not total, because there was one passable road leading towards Zenica, but that was all.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, could I now show a document to the witness. This is D68. For the record, this is a document issued by the Bosnian Krajina RG, Strictly Confidential 09/48-2, dated 27 April [Realtime transcript read in error "February"], 1993. The title is "Regular Combat Rate Fought."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm showing you this document because there are villages mentioned in it. I'm going to quote a segment of that document to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm going to quote the second half of this very short document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The document says: "Minor shooting was heard above Suhi Dol and Zolote, of which HVO members were informed at a joint meeting. Reports from the village of Ricice say that HVO members did not allow villagers to work in the fields." Suhi Dol is actually the place where you resided, where you fought, at the time the document was drafted towards the end of in April of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Members of the HVO did not allow civilian population to move about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They did not allow them to work in the field?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Although, at the time, there were no open conflicts between the two; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my colleague is drawing my attention to the fact that this is a document dating from February 1993, but actually this is a document that was drafted on the 27th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And where does February 1993 come from, then?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know. I suppose this must be an interpretation error. I really don't know where the month of February came from. I have quoted the date on the document, which is the 27th of April, 1993, so I would put it down to misinterpretation. In the transcript, you can see that mistake. The transcript does not reflect my words, and it also doesn't reflect the date indicated in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Where in the --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, line 18, line 19 of the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, that's when you drew our attention to that. You said: "Your Honours, my colleague is drawing my attention to the fact that this is a document dating from February 1993, and," and I'm saying where does it talk of February 1993 before this point?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is on the page at the moment when I was quoting from the document somewhat earlier in the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At page 63, line 24, you said: "Your Honours, I'm going to quote the second half."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And then you say: "the shooting was here above Suhi Dol and Zolote."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, lines 18 and 19 of the LiveNote show a wrong date of the document. Page 63 of the LiveNote. I wanted to correct that mistake. I wanted to put it right and say that the date is 27 April 1993. That is the date when the document was drafted. Your Honours, I apologise. The date of the document is 27 April 1993, and this is what should be recorded in the transcript. The error in the transcript is on page 63, lines 18 and 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, madam. It will be noted as 27th April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your evidence, you spoke about joining a group of Arabs sometime in June 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you also said that, at that time, you didn't need any kind of approval to do so?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, nobody asked me for anything, and I didn't ask anyone anything. I just left.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the way I understood it. If I were to put it to you that the level of organisation in the army in Central Bosnia at that time was at a very low level, you would agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, in my evidence, I already said that part of my motive for going to join the Arabs was because there was no organisation, nobody obeyed anyone, there was no authority, so this was an incentive for me to go there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the way I understand it, fighters left the units whenever they felt like it. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you had to be somewhere, but you could go wherever you wished.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fine, fine. I will now go back to the 306th Brigade. The 306th Brigade was disorganized to such an extent that whole groups of fighters would leave its ranks?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: People left the lines as they went to forage for food because there wasn't enough food to go around?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me now go back to the military police in the 306th Brigade. Would you agree with me that the military police were so few that they couldn't do anything about those transfers?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, they -- they couldn't do anything, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the few military police that were there, it is true that they did not have the weapons and the equipment that would enable them to do their job?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course. Well, the police was there, according to the establishment, but they didn't really perform their duties. Only if somebody would really try to shirk his duties and would not be there for two months, they would go and search for that person.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Generally speaking, the spring and the summer of 1993, that was a time of general chaos in Central Bosnia; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was really, really great chaos. People went hungry. There was uncertainty. We were surrounded on all sides, and there was panic among the people, the sense of insecurity.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I move on to my next question, could we please get an exhibit number for this document that I've just discussed with the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Document D68 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number 100.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to go back to the situation in Central Bosnia at the time when you were in the 306th. You described to us this lack of organisation in very vivid terms. Now, if I were to put it to you that because of this disorganization, there were some internal conflicts, incidents, involving the units of the army at that time, and that this was due to disorganization, there were misunderstandings in which those units clashed by mistake?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's true. I know about one such case. In this action, members of one of our units killed one of our members because they were not familiar with the terrain, those units and those operations were not prepared properly, and this is -- the result was this.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you tell us "our units." By that you mean the 306th or what?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: The 306th and the other units that were there, that participated in this action, the people from Travnik that were heading towards Bukovica, they clashed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And because of this lack of organisation, one man was killed and another was wounded; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me now go back to the foreign fighters. You told us that you had joined a group of Arabs that did not consist of too many members?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, those who existed there at Zapode.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you some questions relating to this group. Sir, could you please explain to the Chamber whether this was the only group of Arabs there in the field or were there some other groups that had nothing to do with this group whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were several groups, not just one. For instance, in Gluha Bukovica, which is again the same area, our area, a group of Arabs were stationed there, they were called the Zubeir's group, and there was another group that took part with us in this operation at Radonjici. I saw those lads from the Turkish guerrilla. There was another group, Abu Ubeidah's group, I knew about them too. They also gathered those people of that kind. They were acting independently, it was a war. It was like the wild west: Might had right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I would like to ask you something in relation to this. These other groups you mentioned, Abu Ubeidah, or Ubeid, the Turkish guerrilla. It is true, is it not, that these people never joined the El Mujahed Detachment; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had their own views that did not correspond to those in El Mujahed, because we, in the detachment, we obeyed discipline. People obeyed the commands. And those who were not willing to do so, they would not be able to exist there. They either would not have lasted long or they wouldn't have joined the detachment because of that situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You knew the situation and the terrain --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a moment. Page 69, line 12 and 13, the witness said "Abu Ubeid" I would like this name to be entered into the transcript properly. You mentioned Abu Ubeid, Witness?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was up there at Buca, at Bijelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see him as a member of the Arab group that you joined?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: No, never. Had those people insisted on it, I would not have joined them ever.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were familiar with the terrain, were you not? Those other groups, do you know whether anyone controlled them?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: No. They could not be controlled. As I explained just a while ago, those who were more persistent, who were willing to cause worse incidents, they ruled. Nobody could fight them. Nobody could even attempt to put them under any control. Nobody dared.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "nobody," I take it that you refer to the units of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Definitely. They wouldn't even dare to look at them, let alone anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you one more question: Did you hear about the camp at Bistricak?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear there was an Iranian training centre in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If somebody were to say that those camps had anything to do with the El Mujahed Detachment, they would not be right?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. They would not be right, 100 per cent sure. The detachment was a disciplined unit. Everybody knew how things are to be done, and nobody wanted to commit any atrocities or any crimes. That would not be acceptable to human beings.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your evidence, you were asked about your reasons, why you joined this group of Arabs, and I would like to ask you some questions about that, too. Do you agree that the people who lived there, the non-Serb population, in particular the Muslim population in Central Bosnia at the time that we're talking about, so it's 1992 and 1993, were in an extremely difficult situation in terms of economy?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They fought for their barest survival?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Exactly. And in that sense, precisely, because nothing could reach us from the outside world. People really went hungry. And then in the spring, people would sow some wheat, and there was some mills, water mills up there, where you could make flour, because that was the only -- the only source of sustenance for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. You will agree with me that people were in a very difficult psychological situation because of the horrors that happened in the field, shelling, people getting killed?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were surrounded by both the Serbs and Croats, and shells could land -- attacks to come from any side; from Vlasic and from the other side, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You saw hundreds of thousands of refugees that flooded Travnik, coming in from Bosnian Krajina and Eastern Bosnia; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The reason why I am asking you this is because I want to find out whether I am correct when I say that in the situation, the people were very prone to turning to religion?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that seemed like the only way out.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you said, in fact, that you joined them for this reason?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And many young Bosnians did that, too, precisely for this reason?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The detachment offered religious education, and that is why the Muslim population - and you told us about their psychological state - found it easy to accept them?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The detachment offered food for the family?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And, for instance, there was no electricity. I remember on one occasion I asked Abu Haris to get me three or four litres of oil, of diesel. I asked for a litres. He gave me more so that we could use it to burn in a lamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your evidence today, you said that when you joined this detachment, or rather, group of Arabs, because you drew this distinction between the period before August and after August; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm asking you about this period where you actually joined this group. You told us that you did not consider that you had left the army ranks, and you clarified what you meant by that. And now I would like to ask you the following question: I conclude that you said this because you consider that you fought the same enemy, that you protected your villages. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was a patriot from Day 1; and, at that time, it was considered that if you joined them, this was like a high-risk unit. They placed more emphasis on fighting, on combat. You were considered to be a better soldier than the ones that were in the 306th.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Fine. But after you left the 306th Brigade, it is true that you did not receive any orders from the brigade during your time when you were with this group of Arabs?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't have any contacts with them at all anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And in this group where you were, together with the Arabs, you did not get any orders from any other unit, the local unit of the Bosnian and Herzegovina Army?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did not receive any such orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You described an engagement today, and I don't know if I understood you correctly. This was a fight in which you were engaged together with this group of Arabs?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is true, at least according to what you know, that you were not summoned to take part in this fight by the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, no suggestion was made to that effect from the 306th. I went there in completely different channels that had nothing to do with 306th.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you something else. It would be fair to say that you heard shooting and you simply joined in the fighting; would that be true? I don't mean you, personally. I mean your group.

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, you could say that. You could describe it that way, because there were no links with anyone, no arrangements -- prior arrangements were made. I learned that we would have -- that we would go into action on the eve of the action itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So I understood that you wanted to say that you learned about the battle just before it actually happened, that it was not your impression that there were no prior arrangements made. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. When we went into action later, we would prepare for at least a month. We would do reconnaissance. This was a spontaneous thing, and I simply joined in; although, this was my first action, and I really didn't do anything to prove my valour. I was a little bit afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you explained to us about this event in June, and you explained things to us on the map, D99. And I would just like to clarify one minor issue here. You described and you mentioned Borovi. Am I right that Borovi is a plateau in the mountains where there are tall pine trees?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There are no habitations there?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yeah, no habitations, just the pinewood.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Prosecutor has also asked you about Isak Aganovic. You don't know whether he was present during events in June in the detachment? Did he participate in the operation?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I said I don't know, and I also said that I didn't even know him at the time. I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I just wanted to make sure. And now I'm going to ask you a few questions relative to the detachment, itself. Is it true that the detachment, between August 1993 and the period thereafter, had a completely different structure and organisation than some other units [as interpreted] of the BiH Army; for example, the one that you had belonged to, the 306th?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to correct something in the LiveNote. Page 76, pages [as interpreted] 1 and 2, I would like to correct myself and say that it had a completely different structure and organisation than the units of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are still on page 75. We're not on page 76 yet. Can you tell us exactly what it is you're correcting? The transcript says you're correcting page 76, and we're still on page 75.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know how. I have page 76 before me. Let me just consult with my case manager to be absolutely sure, and then I'll come back to you. Your Honours, I hope that you have also looked at that. It seems that my transcript is faster than yours. In any case, I would like to correct -- or I have indeed corrected, and that has already been recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but what is the correction? I would like to be with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was speaking about the difference between the detachment and the units of the BiH Army, and the way it was recorded was "between the detachment and another unit of the BiH Army," which is not what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It didn't say "another," it says "and other units of the BiH Army." That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And some other units. I didn't say "some other units." I tried to make a distinction between the BiH Army and the detachment. This would imply that I have put the detachment in the same context with the army. But, Your Honours, in any case, I don't think that this is so important, and I don't wish to spend any more time on it. I don't want to dwell upon it. I would like to remove my remark and move on, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We were talking about the organisation of the detachment, Witness. I asked you this: Did your detachment have an organisation similar to the 306th Brigade that you had been a member of, or was the organisation different?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: In the detachment, we had "surmejs" [phoen], that's what we called them. The leader of the group was an emir. Nobody had ranks. There were no ranks. The man, Muatez, did not have a rank. He was just an emir. That's all he was. Nobody had any ranks. There were no platoons or other such units. There were just groups that bore the leader's name. People were fighting in groups, so the organisation was certainly not the same as it was in the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is true, is it not, that the detachment had a shura; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How would you describe a shura? What was a shura? Can you explain for the Trial Chamber what shura was? Just slowly, please. Slow down and try to do it carefully and slowly. I apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: A shura was made up of several prominent leaders who were decision-makers. They would decide on things; for example, on the further course of actions. If somebody had a proposal, they would decide whether the proposal would be acted upon or not. Some of our men made up our shura.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to ask you this: You probably did not attend the meetings of the shura, but I believe that you knew one thing. And would you agree with me when I say that decisions made by the shura were binding upon the detachment?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't attend any of the meetings, really, but I know that the decisions that were passed by the shura had to be implemented. Whatever proposals had been put forth, if the shura did not make a decision to that effect, we just did not have to do it. Nobody could issue any orders to the detachment if the shura had not approved those orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your explanation, Witness. You were a member of the BiH Army for a while, and you know how it functioned. Would you agree with me that something like a shura did not exist in the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Of course, I agree with you. There was no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness. Your Honours, I would just have a few more questions for this witness about some documents that the Prosecutor used on chief. I would kindly ask the witness to look at an excerpt from Exhibit 78, which is PT2949. Can the witness be shown ERN pages 0365-5062 and 0365-5063. Your Honours, since these pages did not have a translation, we appended our translation to these pages. We were not sure that this would be in the system. I believe that you have these pages in front of you as a hard copy. We have done it electronically, and I believe that we can already see it in e-court as D93. And now I would like the witness to be shown page 0365-5062. Thank you. If possible, could you please blow up the first part of the left side of the document depicting a name.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you agree with me that these are your identification data: Alic, Saban, and the year of birth?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, I would like the witness to be shown page 0365-5063. 0365-5063 is the ERN number of the page. Thank you very much. Again, I would like the court usher to do exactly the same as he did before, i.e., to blow up - thank you very much - the first part of that page. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at the first part of this page, and I am drawing your attention to where it says the military unit, "VJP," and the date, 1st of June, 1993; and below that, you have "VJ" something, unclear. You have the 4th of April, 1992, and a few more on the same page. The first one is legible, and it reads the 1st of June, 1993. Can you see all that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we please have the English version, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see all that?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to ask the usher to blow up the lower portion of the same document, both the English and the Bosnian versions, please. Can you blow up the part with the stamp and the date next to the stamp. Can you please blow up that portion. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, will you agree with me that this document bears the following date: 7 March 1989. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the stamp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. I would like to be with you. Where is this date of 1989; 7 March 1989?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the lower bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, you've seen that, and now can you see that there is a stamp of the Military Post 7719? Please pay attention to the stamp for a moment.

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that the coat of arms is not a coat of arms that was used by the BiH Army during the war; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: This document is from the other army in the former Yugoslavia in the JNA, and this stamp hails from Bor. I was awarded some days off, and I believe that this is the certificate proving that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me, then, that this document originated much before the war, at least two or three years before the beginning of war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now, Your Honours, I would like to ask the usher to blow up the lower portion, the right side of this document. Can you go back a bit more to the right to show the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the date, 15 January 1986, here?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the first part of the document bears the date 15 January 1986? Can you see that? Please look at the document.

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it is even much earlier than you actually started serving in the army?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: That's the time I had still not completed with my regular education.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I have no further questions relative to this question. Thank you. And now can these two pages, with their translation, be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May those two pages, with their translation, please be given an exhibit number. They are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit 101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will have just a couple more questions about Exhibit 67. Can we bring Exhibit 67 on the screen, the first page thereof? Thank you. Can we also have its English translation at the same time? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please look carefully at the document, and do you agree that it says "Receipt" on this document? And also could you please look at the columns and the titles. Does it say "Number,""Quantity," "Title," "Price," "Amount," and the figures are 1 and 6: "Overview of the El Mujahedin Detachment, photocopy"? Do you agree that this is what it reads? Witness, I am sure that you had a plenty of opportunity to purchase things in our country?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I am a tradesman by trade.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you are the right person to explain this document. Do you agree that this document actually looks like a receipt that was issued by a warehouse; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, but there is something else to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: This is even worse than that. This is not a warehouse. I really don't know what that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me take you back to your detachment in August 1993. Witness, please, is it true that the Arabs, i.e., the detachment, had very good equipment, that they even had PCs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They had typewriters?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Among the Muslim members of the detachment, there were those who could use those typewriters?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you ever accept, as a member of the detachment, that such papers were used for receipts in your detachment?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that they were not. I'm positive.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just a few questions to clarify some things on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, you mentioned at page 62, line 18, that Donje Maline had been surrounded. Could you explain to the Court, what is the national or ethnic composition of the majority of people in Donje Maline?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, there's Donje Maline and Gornje Maline. Donje Maline are all Muslims; and in Gornje Maline, they're all Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: It might also be helpful for the benefit of the Trial Chamber to explain what does the word "Donje" before "Maline" mean?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: So, if you're going from the Bila River, you go up towards Maline. First you get to Donje, Lower Maline, and then you go to Gornje, Upper Maline.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Alic. I want to ask you also on page 68, line 13, you mentioned that there was an action that resulted in what is sometimes called "friendly fire" shootings; that is, somebody from your unit or somebody from the ABiH shot another person from the ABiH accidentally?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The transcript wasn't clear. I'd like to clarify. When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: It happened during this action, the action. This group, this unit, the Travnik unit, they were moving in to assist, to give support at Bukovica; and as they linked up with the 306th, they were not in touch. And there had been no prior arrangements made, so shooting ensued and one of -- one of their soldiers was killed and another one was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What month was that?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, it was on that day, the 8th of June. That was on that very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And just to be clear, on the 8th of June is the day that the operation happened that you talked about in your direct examination?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And that was the 8th of June of what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Defence asked you some questions about other groups of foreigners in the area, and she mentioned some names. I'd like to ask you, Witness, were any of these other groups of foreigners ever in the Zapode camp along with you and your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'd also like to clarify. You just mentioned that it was on June 8th, 1993 that this action occurred. Defence indicated that you had joined in June 1993. I just want to be clear. What was the date that you joined the Arabs in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: The 1st of June, the 1st.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And during this operation, did you have command over anybody in the unit?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'd like to ask you a few questions about what now has become marked Exhibit 101. These dates --

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And it might be helpful to pull this up now in e-court. This is 03655062, which is the first of two pages of Exhibit 101.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: There are some dates on the left-hand side of that document, and places. It says: "Kikinda, joined 16/3/1988; and then Bor, 7/12/1988." What do these dates correspond with, and these places, Mr. Alic?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: That means when I went to the army of the former Yugoslavia, I spent six months in Kikinda and then I was transferred to Bor. So I spent the other second half, the second six months, in Bor, which is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: On the next page, 5063, which would be the right-hand side of page 2 of Exhibit 101, which is ERN 0365-5063, there's a date that says "15/1/1986." I wonder, Witness, could you tell the Court how soon before 15/1/1986 you turned 17?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What is your birthday, sir?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: 11th of December, 1969.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia, military service was compulsory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, what were your military obligations after you left the JNA in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I never had any contacts with them whatsoever. As regards the military service, I was not called up to join the reserves. They would sometimes issue those call-up papers for some exercises, but I never went there at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: There was a thing in the former Yugoslavia called "The Territorial Defence," just as there was in the ABiH or the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And do you know, Witness, who was it that maintained the Territorial Defence in the former Yugoslavia? Was it the federal government or the republics?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I think it was all done at the level of the federal state, not at the level of the republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So this document that's marked Exhibit 101, it has information that corresponds with your JNA service?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And it has information that corresponds accurately with your service in the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Just one moment, Your Honour. The Prosecution has nothing further at this time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Wood. Judge. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few questions to ask. This morning, during the examination, you said the soldiers had no discipline, no order, and the brigade was very much disorganized. And one of the reasons, besides religious reasons, the other reason for which you abandoned this brigade and joined the El Mujahedin Unit was this disorganized. You also said that in the El Mujahedin Detachment, you were the best of soldiers. Do you remember what you said about this?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I said that this was the general view among the locals. They considered those who were in the detachment to be better soldiers, in terms of their courage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. And the best soldiers of what army, of which army? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how -- what picture was painted to you of this army. Perhaps you think of the US Marines when you talk about the army, but this was not the case. The army consisted of people wearing civilian clothes or uniforms that were plundered from the warehouses, depots of the former army. And they wore the same kind of pants, the same kind of jackets, and they would put just some new insignia. This was not an army that was established, equipped. It wasn't the case that everybody knew what to do. It looked like a peasant uprising of some sort. If you come under attack, you have to go out, you have to fight. If not, they will come to your home and they will kill you there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, these best soldiers were not part of an army; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were speaking about soldiers. Therefore, soldiers are part of an army, and you said that you were in the El Mujahed Detachment of the best soldiers. After that, you explained to us that those soldiers were not part of an army, if I understood you rightly. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: Well, the establishment existed on paper, but we could not talk about a real army. You have everything on paper; platoons, companies, and so on. This was copied from the former army. But on the field, it just didn't exist the way it was was on paper; and if you told a soldier to do this, he could just not obey you. And what means did you have to force him to obey you? No, none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Perhaps I haven't been very clear. I'm now speaking about your participation to the El Mujahedin Detachment. And it is on this score you said, by making comparison with the soldiers of the 306th Brigade, you said that "in this detachment you were the best soldiers." And when you were part of this detachment, a member of this detachment, you were a soldier of which army? This is what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: I said that the locals thought that if you joined the Arabs, they considered you to be the best soldier. I didn't know what other word to use, so I used the word "soldier." I didn't know how to define this. The locals thought, "Look, he's brave. He dared to go there," because it was riskier if you joined their group. More people got killed there. But the army, I am not trying to put anyone down here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Another small point. In this detachment, did you have a radio or a telephone to communicate with other combat units or with command, both, of any kind?

utterances.speaker: SABIN ALIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, nobody had any radio stations or communicated in this way with anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. We obviously have gone past the time. We'll have to adjourn to tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning at Courtroom I. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: For the English transcript, the interpreter requests that the word "counter-exam" or "counter-examination" be changed into "cross-examination." Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
